SECTION 1 — AYURVEDA FUNDAMENTALS
1.1 What is Ayurveda?
Ayurveda (from Sanskrit āyus, “life” or “longevity,” and veda, “knowledge” or
“science”) is one of the world’s oldest documented systems of medicine and
wellbeing, originating on the Indian subcontinent. It is recognized in India as one of
the officially supported Indian Systems of Medicine, alongside Yoga, Unani, Siddha,

the officially supported Indian Systems of Medicine, alongside Yoga, Unani, Siddha,
Sowa-Rigpa, and Homoeopathy, collectively administered under the Ministry of
AYUSH.
Traditional claim: Ayurveda describes itself as a comprehensive system covering
diet, lifestyle, herbal and mineral formulations, detoxification and rejuvenation
procedures (Panchakarma), surgery (as historically described in the Sushruta
Samhita), and preventive and promotive health practices, aimed at maintaining

Samhita), and preventive and promotive health practices, aimed at maintaining
balance between mind, body, and environment.
Scientific evidence: Modern biomedical science evaluates Ayurvedic concepts and
formulations using its own separate frameworks (pharmacology, clinical trials,
toxicology). Some individual Ayurvedic herbs and formulations have been studied
using modern scientific methods with mixed and formulation-specific results;

using modern scientific methods with mixed and formulation-specific results;
Ayurveda as a whole system has not been validated or invalidated as a single unit by
modern science, because its foundational concepts (doshas, dhatus) are not
framework-equivalent to biomedical categories. Claims of efficacy for any specific
condition should be verified against current peer-reviewed literature and regulatory
assessments rather than assumed from tradition alone.

1.2 Historical Background
• Ayurvedic concepts are traceable to ancient Sanskrit textual traditions, with
foundational compilations conventionally dated to roughly the first
millennium BCE through the early centuries CE, though exact dating of oral-
to-written transmission is debated among historians.
• Ayurveda developed alongside other Indian intellectual traditions
(philosophy, surgery, chemistry/alchemy known as Rasashastra) and was

(philosophy, surgery, chemistry/alchemy known as Rasashastra) and was
transmitted through teacher-student (guru-shishya) lineages, temple and
monastic institutions, and family/community practice.
• During the colonial period, institutional support for Ayurveda in India
declined relative to Western biomedicine; post-independence India took
steps to formally recognize and regulate Ayurveda through dedicated
statutes, education boards, and eventually a dedicated ministry (Ministry of

statutes, education boards, and eventually a dedicated ministry (Ministry of
AYUSH, elevated to a full ministry in 2014 [VERIFY]).
• Today Ayurveda is practiced in India under statutory regulation (registered
practitioners, accredited colleges) and has also spread internationally as a
complementary/alternative medicine system, subject to the medical-practice
and product-safety laws of each country.

1.4 Basic Concepts of Ayurveda
The following are traditional Ayurvedic concepts. They are described here as they
appear in Ayurvedic theory; they are not biomedical diagnostic categories.
1.4.1 Doshas: Vata, Pitta, Kapha
Traditional claim: Ayurveda describes three fundamental physiological principles

Traditional claim: Ayurveda describes three fundamental physiological principles
called doshas, said to govern bodily and mental functions:
• Vata — associated with movement, the nervous system, circulation, and
elimination; traditionally linked to the elements air and space/ether.
• Pitta — associated with metabolism, digestion, and transformation;
traditionally linked to the elements fire and water.
• Kapha — associated with structure, lubrication, and stability; traditionally

• Kapha — associated with structure, lubrication, and stability; traditionally
linked to the elements earth and water.
Ayurvedic theory holds that each individual has a unique baseline proportion of the
three doshas and that disease arises from imbalance among them. This is a
traditional explanatory framework, not a scientifically validated physiological model
in the biomedical sense.
1.4.2 Dhatus
Traditional claim: Dhatus are the seven traditional “tissues” said to sustain the

1.4.2 Dhatus
Traditional claim: Dhatus are the seven traditional “tissues” said to sustain the
body: Rasa (plasma/nutrient fluid), Rakta (blood), Mamsa (muscle), Meda (fat),
Asthi (bone), Majja (marrow/nervous tissue), and Shukra (reproductive tissue).
1.4.3 Malas
Traditional claim: Malas are the traditional waste products of metabolism —
principally Purisha (feces), Mutra (urine), and Sweda (sweat) — whose proper
elimination is considered necessary for health.

1.4.4 Prakriti
Traditional claim: Prakriti refers to an individual’s inherent constitutional type,
determined (according to Ayurvedic theory) at conception by the relative
proportion of the three doshas, and considered relatively fixed for life. Ayurvedic
practice traditionally uses assessment of Prakriti to guide individualized dietary and
lifestyle recommendations. This is a traditional classificatory concept and is distinct

lifestyle recommendations. This is a traditional classificatory concept and is distinct
from, and should not be confused with, genetic or genomic classification in modern
biology.

Distinguishing traditional knowledge from modern scientific evidence
(general principle for this entire document): A traditional preparation method
or use being centuries old does not, by itself, establish that the preparation is safe,
effective, or free of contamination by modern regulatory standards. Conversely, a
preparation being traditional does not mean it lacks value — it means the claim

preparation being traditional does not mean it lacks value — it means the claim
should be evaluated on its own evidentiary merits (toxicology, clinical data,
regulatory approval) rather than by appeal to tradition or by dismissal of tradition.
This distinction is central to Sections 2–5 of this document, which examine how
traditional use interacts with patent law (as prior art) rather than with medical
claims.

SECTION 2 — TRADITIONAL KNOWLEDGE
2.1 Definition of Traditional Knowledge
“Traditional Knowledge” (TK) does not have one single, universally binding legal
definition, but it is generally understood — including in WIPO’s work — as

definition, but it is generally understood — including in WIPO’s work — as
knowledge, know-how, skills, and practices that are developed, sustained, and
passed down from generation to generation within a community, often forming part
of its cultural or spiritual identity. TK can relate to agriculture, the environment,
healthcare (including Ayurveda and other traditional medicine systems),
biodiversity-related knowledge, and traditional/cultural expressions.

biodiversity-related knowledge, and traditional/cultural expressions.
[VERIFY] Because there is no single global treaty definition of TK currently in force
(as opposed to ongoing negotiations — see Section 9), the precise legal scope of
“traditional knowledge” can differ between national laws and international
discussions. Any project relying on a specific legal definition should identify which
law or instrument’s definition is being used.

law or instrument’s definition is being used.
2.2 Traditional Knowledge Associated with Biological Resources
A large share of TK relevant to Ayurveda is TK associated with genetic/biological
resources — i.e., knowledge about the properties or uses of a specific plant, animal,
or microorganism (for example, that a particular plant’s leaves can be used for a
particular purpose). This category is significant because:
• It sits at the intersection of two international frameworks: intellectual

• It sits at the intersection of two international frameworks: intellectual
property law (patents) and biodiversity law (access and benefit-sharing,
discussed in Section 9).
• It is the category most often implicated in “biopiracy” disputes, because a
patent claim on a plant-based invention can be undermined or supported by
evidence of pre-existing traditional use.
2.3 Traditional Medicinal Knowledge
Traditional medicinal knowledge specifically encompasses documented and

Traditional medicinal knowledge specifically encompasses documented and
undocumented knowledge of diagnostic methods, treatments, formulations, and
health practices originating in traditional medicine systems (in India, principally
Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, and Sowa-Rigpa, alongside Yoga). It exists in two broad
forms:
1. Documented traditional knowledge — recorded in classical texts,
manuscripts, government publications, or scholarly compilations. This is

manuscripts, government publications, or scholarly compilations. This is
generally easier to use as documentary prior art in a patent proceeding
because it has an identifiable publication date and source.
2. Oral/undocumented traditional knowledge — held within communities,
families, or individual practitioners without a formal written record. This is
traditionally harder to use as patent prior art because patent law in most

traditionally harder to use as patent prior art because patent law in most
jurisdictions requires evidence of what was “publicly known” or “publicly
used” as of a certain date, and undocumented oral knowledge can be difficult
to prove or date with the evidentiary certainty patent offices require.
2.4 Community Knowledge
Community knowledge refers to TK held collectively by an identifiable community
(e.g., an indigenous or tribal community, or a defined local/traditional occupational

(e.g., an indigenous or tribal community, or a defined local/traditional occupational
group) rather than by an individual inventor. This collective character creates
specific legal and ethical challenges:
• Conventional IP law (patents, copyright) is generally built around identifiable
individual or corporate authorship/inventorship and a fixed term of
protection, which fits awkwardly with knowledge that is collectively held,

protection, which fits awkwardly with knowledge that is collectively held,
continuously evolving, and intended to be perpetual rather than time-limited.
• This mismatch is a central reason why specialized “sui generis” (custom-built)
legal approaches to protecting TK have been proposed and, in some
countries, adopted, rather than relying solely on existing IP categories (see
Section 9).

2.5 Oral and Documented Traditional Knowledge — Why the Distinction
Matters for IP
The oral/documented distinction (introduced in 2.3) has direct legal consequences:
• For defensive protection (stopping wrongful patents), documented TK is
far more useful because it can be cited as prior art with a verifiable date and
source (this is the entire logic behind TKDL — see Section 3).
• For positive protection (giving TK holders enforceable rights over their

• For positive protection (giving TK holders enforceable rights over their
own knowledge), documentation can sometimes cut both ways — it makes
the knowledge easier to prove, but publishing knowledge that was previously
restricted or sacred can also mean giving up practical control over it, since
published information generally cannot later be “taken back” into
confidentiality.

2.6 Problems Caused by Unauthorized Commercialization
2.6.1 Biopiracy
“Biopiracy” is a widely used but legally informal term (it does not appear as a
defined term in most national statutes) referring to situations where biological
resources and/or associated traditional knowledge are accessed, used, or patented
— typically by a foreign company, research institution, or government — without
adequate prior informed consent from, or benefit-sharing with, the country or

adequate prior informed consent from, or benefit-sharing with, the country or
community that is the source of the resource or knowledge. Common features cited
in biopiracy disputes include:
• Patents claiming a “new” use, extract, or method that closely tracks a pre-
existing traditional use.
• Access to biological material or associated knowledge without the consent
required under applicable biodiversity-access law.
• Commercialization proceeding without any agreed benefit-sharing

• Commercialization proceeding without any agreed benefit-sharing
arrangement with the country of origin or knowledge-holding community.
2.6.2 Misappropriation of Traditional Knowledge
“Misappropriation” in this context generally refers to the unauthorized taking, use,
or commercial exploitation of TK contrary to the customary norms of the
community that holds it, or without the legally required consent/benefit-sharing
where such requirements exist. Whether a specific instance amounts to

where such requirements exist. Whether a specific instance amounts to
misappropriation as a matter of law depends on the applicable jurisdiction’s rules
(e.g., India’s Biological Diversity Act — see Section 6) and on the facts of the case;
the term is used loosely in policy debate as well as more precisely in specific
statutes.

LIBRARY (TKDL)
3.1 What is TKDL?
The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) is a digital, structured database
of publicly available traditional knowledge relating to Indian systems of medicine,
created and maintained by India’s Council of Scientific and Industrial Research

created and maintained by India’s Council of Scientific and Industrial Research
(CSIR) in collaboration with the Ministry of AYUSH. It converts information from
classical and other public-domain texts on Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa,
and Yoga into a searchable digital format, classified using a purpose-built
classification system (the Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification, TKRC) and
translated into multiple languages (English, French, German, Spanish, and Japanese)

translated into multiple languages (English, French, German, Spanish, and Japanese)
so that patent examiners in other countries can search and understand it.
3.2 Why TKDL Was Created
TKDL was created in direct response to a recurring problem: patent applications
were being filed and, in some cases, granted in other countries for uses of Indian
medicinal plants (such as turmeric and neem) that already existed as traditional

medicinal plants (such as turmeric and neem) that already existed as traditional
knowledge in India, but that traditional knowledge had not been accessible to patent
examiners in a form they could search — because it existed mainly in Sanskrit, Hindi,
Urdu, Arabic, Tamil, and other languages, in texts not indexed in the patent
classification systems examiners normally use. TKDL was designed to close this
“language and format” gap so that genuine prior art could be found before a patent is

“language and format” gap so that genuine prior art could be found before a patent is
granted, rather than only after (which requires expensive opposition or re-
examination proceedings, as happened in the turmeric and neem cases described in
Section 10).
3.3 History and Purpose
• TKDL was established in 2001 by CSIR in collaboration with (what is now)
the Ministry of AYUSH.
• Its stated core objective is defensive protection: to prevent the wrongful

the Ministry of AYUSH.
• Its stated core objective is defensive protection: to prevent the wrongful
grant of patents on inventions that are, in substance, already part of India’s
traditional knowledge, by making that knowledge available as searchable
prior art to patent examiners worldwide.
• Over time, TKDL has entered into TKDL Access (Non-Disclosure) Agreements
with patent offices in multiple countries and regions, allowing examiners at

with patent offices in multiple countries and regions, allowing examiners at
those offices to search the TKDL database (subject to confidentiality
restrictions) during examination of relevant applications.

3.4 How Traditional Knowledge is Documented in TKDL
TKDL’s methodology, at a general level, involves:
1. Identifying source texts already in the public domain (classical Ayurveda,
Unani, Siddha, and Sowa-Rigpa texts, and Yoga-related texts).
2. Extracting discrete “shlokas”/formulations/statements of use from those
texts.
3. Structuring each entry with standardized fields (e.g., ingredient, disease/use

texts.
3. Structuring each entry with standardized fields (e.g., ingredient, disease/use
category, method of preparation) using the Traditional Knowledge Resource
Classification (TKRC), a classification system created specifically because
existing international patent classification systems (like the IPC) did not have
adequate categories for traditional medicine subject matter.
4. Translating entries into the five languages listed above.

4. Translating entries into the five languages listed above.
5. Making the database available to partner patent offices under non-disclosure
terms (to prevent the underlying traditional knowledge itself from being
taken and misused, while still letting examiners use it to identify lack of
novelty).
3.5 How TKDL Helps Prevent Wrongful Patent Claims
TKDL operates as a form of defensive protection (a concept discussed generally in

TKDL operates as a form of defensive protection (a concept discussed generally in
Section 9): rather than seeking to grant TK holders new exclusive rights, it works by
ensuring that patent examiners can find pre-existing traditional knowledge as prior
art during the routine examination of a patent application. If an examiner finds that
the “invention” being claimed is already described in a TKDL entry, that finding can

the “invention” being claimed is already described in a TKDL entry, that finding can
be used to reject the application for lack of novelty or inventive step (see Section 5
on patentability requirements), ideally before a patent is ever granted — avoiding
the need for the costly, multi-year opposition or re-examination proceedings that
were required in cases like the turmeric and neem patents.
3.6 Relationship Between TKDL and Patent Examination

3.6 Relationship Between TKDL and Patent Examination
• TKDL is a search and reference tool for examiners , not a legal register of
ownership and not itself a form of intellectual property protection for the TK
it documents.
• TKDL does not, by itself, stop a patent office from granting a patent; it
depends on the examiner actually searching and correctly applying the TKDL
prior art during examination, or on affected parties citing TKDL material
during opposition.

during opposition.
• Access is generally structured under confidentiality agreements to strike a
balance: examiners can use the content to assess novelty, but the traditional
knowledge itself (much of which is culturally significant and, in some
communities’ view, should not be freely commercially exploited) is not
thereby placed in an unrestricted public database beyond what is already
public domain.

SECTION 4 — INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY BASICS
4.1 What is Intellectual Property?
Intellectual Property (IP) refers to a category of legally recognized rights over
creations of the mind — inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, symbols,
names, and certain confidential information — that allow the rights-holder to

names, and certain confidential information — that allow the rights-holder to
control specific uses of that creation for a defined period (or, for some categories
such as trade secrets and some trademarks, potentially indefinitely provided
conditions are maintained). IP rights are territorial (granted and enforced on a
country-by-country or region-by-region basis, subject to international treaties that
harmonize certain minimum standards).

In simple terms: a patent is a deal between an inventor and the government. The

others from making, using, selling, or importing that invention for a limited time (in

5.2 What is a Patent? (Technical explanation)
A patent is a statutory, territorial, negative right — it does not itself grant the
patentee a positive right to practice the invention (which may still be restricted by
other laws), but it grants the right to exclude others from making, using, selling,

The invention must not have been disclosed to the public, anywhere in the world, in
any form (written, oral, use, or otherwise) before the patent application’s filing date
(or valid priority date). Existing disclosures that defeat novelty are called prior art.
5.3.2 Inventive Step (Non-Obviousness)
The invention must not be obvious to a “person skilled in the art” (a hypothetical

The invention must not be obvious to a “person skilled in the art” (a hypothetical

of the prior art existing at the relevant date. A small, predictable modification of

5.3.3 Industrial Applicability (Utility)
The invention must be capable of being made or used in some kind of industry, i.e., it

The invention must be capable of being made or used in some kind of industry, i.e., it
must have a practical, working application rather than being purely theoretical or

5.3.4 Sufficiency of Disclosure
The patent application must describe the invention clearly and completely enough
that a person skilled in the art could reproduce it, and must include claims that
define the precise scope of protection sought.
